native component FlatString

import String.{maxLeafSize, concatAndBalanceIfNecessary, CatString, spaces}
import Stream.{...}

export FlatString


private language="java"
private package="com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim"

lineSeparator: String = LineSeparator()

private natLineSeparator(): String = builtinPrimitive(
            "com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.lineSeparator")

private LineSeparator(): String =do
    ignore(FlatString); (* This initializes the constructor for FlatString
                   before its type is used (in the next line). *)
    natLineSeparator()
  end

object FlatString extends { String, DelegatedIndexed⟦Char, ZZ32⟧ }
    getter size() : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeStrlen")
    getter asExprString() : String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.asExprString")
    getter asFlatString(): String = self
    getter asString(): String = self
    getter asDebugString(): String = asDebugStringIndented(0)
    getter depth():ZZ32 = 0

    (* With the help of trait DelegatedIndex, this defines our generate method *)
    getter generator() : Generator⟦Char⟧ =
        self.indices.map⟦Char⟧(fn (i:ZZ32):Char ⇒ self.get(i))

    getter isBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isAlmostBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isExtremelyUnbalanced():Boolean = false

    balanced():String = self

    opr |self| : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeStrlen")

    uncheckedSubstring(r1: Range⟦ZZ32⟧) : String = do
    (* We could build a subString node here, but not until everything is working,
        because that will introduce
       SubString objects into code that may still expect FlatStrings.
       As written, this method always answers a FlatString.
       In any case, the FlatString object supports substring without copying*)
        assert((r1 ∩ self.bounds).isEmpty, r1.isEmpty,
                    "Empty substring of non-empty string")
        if r1.isEmpty then ""
        else self.javaSubstr(r1.left.get, r1.right.get + 1)    (* Java substr's endIndex is one past the last character *)
        end
    end

    opr =(self, other: FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.stringEquals")
    opr <(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) < 0
    opr <=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≤ 0
    opr >(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) > 0
    opr >=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≥ 0
    opr CMP(self, other: FlatString): TotalComparison =  self.cmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CMP(self, other:String):TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CMP self)
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:FlatString): TotalComparison =
      self.cicmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:String): TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP self)

    (** get skips bounds checking. **)
    get(i:ZZ32): Char =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.charAt")
    cmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.compareTo")
    cicmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.compareToIgnoreCase")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32,hi:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.javaSubstr")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32): String = javaSubstr(lo, self.size)
    javaIndexOf(c:Char): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.indexOf")
    flatConcat(self, b:FlatString):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeConcatenate")
    flatConcat(self, b:Char):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeConcatenateChar")
    javaRegExpMatches(m:FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.javaRegExpMatches")
    javaRegExpSplit(m:FlatString, i:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.javaRegExpSplit")

    indexOf(c:Char): Maybe⟦ZZ32⟧ = do
        i = javaIndexOf(c)
        if i = -1 then Nothing⟦ZZ32⟧ else Just⟦ZZ32⟧(i) end
      end

    verify():() = do
        assert(self.depth, 0, self)
    end

    asDebugStringIndented(indent: ZZ32): String =
        spaces(indent) || "J" |self| "/" self.depth ":" self

    opr ∈(c:Char, self): Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ≠ -1

    rangeContains(r: Range⟦ZZ32⟧, c: Char):Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ∈ self.bounds[r]

    (** The operator %||% with at least one String argument converts to string and
        concatenates **)
    opr ||(self, b:FlatString): String = do
        if b.isEmpty then self
        elif self.size + b.size > maxLeafSize then
             (* Since both self and b have depth 0, balancing can't be necessary *)
            CatString(self, b)
        else
            flatConcat(self, b)
        end
      end

    opr ||(self, b:String):String = do
        if self.isEmpty then b
        elif b.isEmpty then self
        elif self.size + b.size > maxLeafSize then
            concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b)
        else
            typecase b.asFlatString of
                f:FlatString ⇒ flatConcat(self, f)
                f:String ⇒ concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b)
            end
        end
    end

    opr ||(self, b:Char): String =
        if |self| ≥ maxLeafSize then
            concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b.asString)
        else
            flatConcat(self, b)
        end

    splitWithOffsets():ZeroIndexed⟦(ZZ32, String)⟧ = Nothing⟦(ZZ32, String)⟧
    split():Generator⟦String⟧ = Nothing⟦String⟧

    writeOn(stream: WriteStream): () = stream.write(self)

end FlatString

end

content.content:
## A small change to the existing process

Replace the post-landing update instruction with a rule of this form:

> After a landing, update the skill where the landed tree changes what a worker must understand or do. Rewrite the existing explanation of that subject. State the current rule, its scope and the exceptions needed to use it. Keep a short contrast with the original Fortress only when it prevents a likely mistake. Put the repair history and supporting evidence in sources and reports. A landing does not require a new Revival entry.

Use the same intent in the writer's brief and Revival's introduction. Otherwise the old “each change” instruction remains a competing requirement. This is a proposed change of policy for approval, not a wording correction already applied.

Within the existing writer task:

1. Identify the current guidance affected by the landed findings. Decide whether to replace it, add a necessary qualification, link to its existing home, or make no skill change.
2. State the resulting rule without the batch narrative. Preserve path and library differences. An unresolved gap is current information when it changes how a worker must act.
3. Update sources for each changed rule. Use the guidance heading and exact evidence location. Keep the maintained text understandable without that evidence file.
4. Check nearby guidance and other entries that state the same behaviour. Do this by bounded search, not a whole-corpus rewrite.

In the existing cold read, add two questions:

> What would you do differently after reading this section? State the rule and its limits without opening the sources.

> Does this section contain repair history or detail that changes no action and prevents no misunderstanding?

The writer's evidence check remains separate. Retain the existing consolidation question:

> **Does this summary let a reader conclude more than the evidence establishes?**

Do not turn “no search” into “include every detail”. A worker should not need sources to understand the skill's rule. It can still follow a clear link to another skill part or a detailed report when its task requires that detail.

## Example of the boundary

The sampled “An integer power” entry mixes the current power rule with earlier behaviour, changed demo filenames, the `strToInt` repair, typed `fail`, api repairs and differences between the two libraries.

The essential current explanation is that integer power in the interpreter's library preserves the base type, including defined exceptional behaviour at negative exponents. A float or rational base is needed for fractional results. The compiler-library and `IntLiteral` exceptions must remain visible: removing those would widen the claim incorrectly.

The list of demos rewritten from `10^(-k)` to `10.0^(-k)` is repair history. Keep it in the report or sources. The typed `fail` rule is independently useful, but belongs with result typing or library-writing guidance, not buried inside integer power. Link to that home if necessary. This is selection and relocation, not deletion of evidence.

Use this one entry as a trial before rewriting the whole file. Verify that the shorter version preserves the operational distinctions and that its sources still support them. Then apply the same boundary to one topic section. Compare length and cold-reader answers; length alone is not success.

------
## Recovered admission rule, workflow runs and transcript search pointers

Follow-up on October 22: the curator clarified that each Revival entry must earn its place by correcting a worker's default mental model to match **revived Fortress**. This is an admission test for each addition or edit, and a retention test during consolidation, not merely a final readability check.

### The original rule is on record

`explorations/reviews/skills-review-style.md`, Lens 10, gives the test verbatim:

> Test: name an agent that acts differently without the sentence. Name the record or transcript that shows the failure. If there is neither, cut it.

The same review records the curator's October 8 goal: use the agents' pretraining knowledge to guide them toward a correct mental model of Fortress. Section 2, M3 links that goal to the pretraining quiz and distillation audit. M4 records the October 5 05:54 request for a fresh reader and scenarios containing traps; it says this became cold reads given only the skill, followed by fixes and work on triggering/routing. Those times are as recorded in the artifact; their timezone was not independently verified.

This is stronger recovered support than the general “flag gotchas” instruction alone. The writer should require a default assumption, the correction for revived Fortress, and the consequential mistake avoided. Keep supporting evidence in sources or the evaluation record, not as another compulsory three-part paragraph in Revival.

### Actual automated work, distinguished from the unverified paired test

| Artifact | What it establishes |
|---|---|
| `explorations/reviews/fortress-repo-rewrite-points.md`, opening | A completed rewrite Workflow run, **`wf_185878c8-0fb`**, on October 8: sixteen writers, one per part, then three cold readers and fixes. Commits: `24af7743b` rewrite, `9a9c30d95` cold-read fixes, `cae2a0ad5` comparison. |

Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has integer powers only at `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64`, each with an exponent of its own type; its `RR64` power takes an `RR64` or a `ZZ32` exponent, a negative one included. Its `ZZ32` power gives 0 at a negative exponent for other bases. At a base of 0 it throws a Java exception that no `catch` sees (rows 441, 523).
102	
103	**`/` on two integers answers a `QQ`.** So `7 / 2` is `7/2`, not 3. Truncate with `DIV`, on both paths. `DIV` answers its operands' type and rounds toward zero. For a float, make one operand a float, as `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` values `s` and `n`. No coercion carries a `ZZ64` into `RR64`, so convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64`, so a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error.
104	
105	## Reductions and comprehensions
106	
107	A clause form is a reduction or comprehension with generators in brackets, as `SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)`.
108	
109	**A reduction's static argument depends on the path.** The checker does not infer it for `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`, whose bound names the parameter (row 731). Write it in every clause form, as `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Other reductions take their bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit. Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's return type, also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a field, a top-level variable, a parameter and an assignment do not direct it. Else walk takes the join of the elements' run-time types. If that join is outside the reduction's bound, each `+` runs at its operands' types. An element that does not convert to the instance stops in `__bigOperator`, "body param 1". Departures under walk:
110	
111	- with no declared type, an empty `SUM` gives the integer 0 (row 716);
112	- a comprehension inside another clause form is built at its elements' run-time types (row 717);
113	- a written static argument that is not a number type ends an empty `SUM` in `CastError` (row 436).
114	
115	**A reduction without an identity lifts its elements to `Maybe[\R\]` inside the reduction.** `BIG MIN`, `BIG MAX` and the string reduction `BIG //` extend `AssociativeReduction[\R\]`, whose `simpleJoin` takes and answers `R`. `BIG MAX` over a generator still answers `R`. Walk refuses at load a reduction without static parameters that declares `simpleJoin` at `Any` or untyped. A generic one stops at its first join. The team's tests declare `simpleJoin` so: do not copy them.
116	
117	## Implementation limits
118	
119	**Walk has no static types.** Walk will run the checker only after the switch-over (P-12). So walk runs programs that the checker refuses. Besides a `Boolean`, it takes a `Maybe` as an `if` condition, `Just` as true and `Nothing` as false. It refuses any other value. The specification and the checker take only a `Boolean`, so do not write a `Maybe` condition. The compiled path's own limits are in `compiler.md`.
120	
121	**Write every parameter type.** The compiled path refuses a parameter without a type, of a function, a method or a local function: "Missing parameter type for". Walk runs it, except in a method that implements an abstract one (row 405). A component's function that leaves out its return type takes the api's declaration at its parameter types. With none or several, the checker types the body.

usage: facts-extract.sh [--check] [--part N] [--page-bytes N] [--root DIR] [--common] [QUERY ...]

Prints what the queries name, whole and in the order they are given; a rung's
briefing is one such command. Each piece comes under a line naming its file
and section. The output comes in parts of at most PAGE_BYTES (default 28000);
part 1 opens with the size of the whole output in bytes and estimated tokens,
then what was asked for, where it is and what was not found; each part says
whether there is a next one, and --part N prints part N.

QUERY is one of:
  F-87, P-48             the entry of that number in FACTS.md or POSITIONS.md
  F-87+                  the entry, then each entry it points to and each entry
                         that points to it, each once, one level
  history:F-87           the entry's blocks in FACTS-history.md or
                         POSITIONS-history.md, oldest first: the provenance line
                         of each change and the line it replaced
  TITLE                  the FACTS.md entry whose title holds TITLE: an entry's
                         title is its bold opening, or where it has none, its
                         opening words up to the first colon, semicolon or full
                         stop; when no current title holds it, the entry one of
                         whose former titles (in FACTS-history.md) does, with a
                         line saying it was retitled
  section:HEADING        every entry of the FACTS.md section whose heading holds HEADING
  index:WORDS            the INDEX.md lines that hold every one of WORDS (at most 10)
  ledger:ROW             row ROW of the gap ledger, whole, under its section and
                         the table's header
  ledger-find:WORDS      one line for each gap ledger row that holds every one of
                         WORDS: its number, its status and the first 150 characters
                         of its claim (at most 10, then how many more matched)
  positions:TITLE        the entry of POSITIONS.md whose bold title holds TITLE, as
                         a TITLE query does in FACTS.md, former titles included;
                         exactly one must, else the nearest titles are named
  positions:DATE WORDS   the entry of POSITIONS.md dated DATE (YYYY-MM-DD, the first
                         date in the entry) whose head, the entry's text up to its
                         first colon and space, holds every one of WORDS; when no
                         entry of POSITIONS.md matches, the entry of
                         POSITIONS-history.md, from the latest of its sections
                         that hold one, with the line saying what became of
                         it; the output says which file it came from
  map:FILE#HEADING       the section of explorations/coordinator/map/FILE whose
                         heading holds HEADING, down to the next heading of its level
  doc:PATH#HEADING       the same for any note, PATH from the repository root, such
                         as a judge's ruling; doc:PATH alone prints the whole note;
                         in a .tex or .tick file the headings are its \chapter, \section,
                         \subsection, \subsubsection and \paragraph titles,
                         matched with their macros dropped; a heading equal to
                         HEADING wins over the headings that merely hold it, and
                         HEADING may be a path, A > B, for B's section inside A's
  map:FILE#HEADING@WORDS, doc:PATH#HEADING@WORDS
                         only the table rows and list items of that section that
                         hold every one of WORDS, a row under its table's header,
                         and the paragraphs whose bold lead holds them
  code:PATH#FROM         the declaration that starts on the one line of PATH that
                         holds FROM, with its line numbers: in .java, .scala and
                         .js through the brace that closes it, elsewhere (.fss,
                         .fsi) through its more indented lines and its end
  code:PATH#FROM..TO     from the declaration at FROM through the end of the
                         one at the first line after it that holds TO
WORDS match as whole words, or as the start of one when a word ends in *.
Matching ignores case, backticks and double quotes, reads curly quotes as

### A (`rung-static-numerals`, `a26e74f5c8`)

**The change.** The team's compiled path typed a numeral by its prelude's `IntLiteral` or `FloatLiteral` and converted it when the program ran: its code generator emitted an `FIntLiteral` value and a call of the prelude's `coerce_ZZ32` on it at each evaluation, the pair its bytecode optimizer's `RemoveLiteralCoercions` pass matched (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/asmbytecodeoptimizer/RemoveLiteralCoercions.java:33-51` at b5b0f82c13; `compiler/runtimeValues/FIntLiteral.java` at b5b0f82c13). Now no numeral value exists at run time on the compiled path: each place of a numeral holds one value made before the program runs, a JVM constant where the compile-time evaluation of the place's type's own coercion from the numeral's type ends in an `int`, `long`, `float` or `double` (`ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `RR32`, `RR64`), and otherwise a static final filled once when the component's class loads, by one call of that coercion compiled as a method of the numeral's four numbers as `ZZ` values (`ZZ`, a program's own types); a place whose type names a type parameter of its generic declaration still calls that method at each evaluation (row 957), and a coercion whose body spawns a task fails the class's load (row 971). A program's type's prefix minus on a negative constant runs once in that static final. Under walk, a folded constant at a library number type converts from its exact value. Tests: `ProjectFortress/library_tests/NumeralFoldIntegers.test`, `NumeralFoldFloats.test`, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/NumeralAcrossComponent.test`, `NumeralMinusOnceCompiled.test`, `NumeralCoercionOnceCompiled.test`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/desugarer/NumeralCoercionFoldJUTest.java`, `ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralFoldedConstantLibraryWalk.fss`. The reason: the Working Draft gives numerals types of their own so that "library designers [can] decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations", and has the libraries define the coercions into the number types (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-148`); a numeral's coercion called at run time per numeral failed for a coercion of another component, "java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: NumeralAcrossComponentApi$v".

**Provenance.** P-174 and P-176, and the snapshot's section 11 on the library's own types (`explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-11-09-numerals/design-snapshot.md`); forks A1 (the fold over a closed fragment), A2 (one method per numeral coercion), A3 (folded constants from their exact value) and A8 (the deleted classes) of climb batch 29b's record; the static numerals probe's patch; rung A of climb batch 29b.

### T (`rung-static-numerals-spec`, `fcfd0aeb31`)

**The change.**
- The team's source: the Working Draft gives a numeral six types, `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]` (and `Literal[\v\]` without leading zeros), `NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix[\n,r,v\]`, `RadixPointNumeral[\n,m,10,v\]`, `RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix[\n,m,r,v\]` and `Numeral[\n,m,r,v\]` above all (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`), says that "Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types" (`:132-141`) and that libraries define coercions from numerals (`:146-148`), and says nothing of a numeral's value when a program runs or of when a coercion is applied. The team's compiled library types numerals by run-time values, `trait IntLiteral` and `trait FloatLiteral` with getters such as `asZZ32` and `asRR64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:390`, `:479`, at b5b0f82c13), whose coercions run on that value.
- What the text now says: a numeral's type exists only at compile time, `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]` or `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]`, at the Draft's arities with the radix as `r`, below a `Numeral` without static parameters; the explicit-radix types and `Literal` are not built; no value of a numeral type exists when a program runs, so a numeral type has no method, no `asFloat` and no `=` with a number type; every number type, the library's and a program's, takes a numeral through `coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\])` or its radix-point form, whose body reads the four numbers as `ZZ` values; the compiler folds it to a constant, or makes the value once per place; `-3` at a program's type is the type's own `-` on the coercion's result for `3`; a `where` clause over the four numbers refuses a numeral statically (`Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:98-285`; `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:5010-5486`). The tests that show the tree doing so land with the code: `ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralStaticDesignWalk.fss`, `ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralOwnTypeWalk.fss`, `ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralTypeNoValueWalk.fss`, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/NumeralStaticDesignCompiled.fss` and `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXNumeralWhereRefusedCompiled.test`.

content.content:
Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. Walk has no static types, so it cannot choose statically. The expected-failure tests `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss` and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss` record the difference.

Walk departs from the rules of `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways, until each fix lands. A test of one of these cases asserts the rules' answer, as an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`), unless the case says otherwise.

- A float numeral to the left of an `RR32` operand runs `RR64`'s operator: for `a: RR32`, `2.5 + a` is an `RR64`, and `a + 2.5` an `RR32` (ledger row 958). Bind the numeral at `RR32` first, as `c: RR32 = 2.5`, then write `c + a`.
- A numeral with a radix point keeps only one of its leading zeros, so its `digits` getter gives 2 for `00.5`, not 3 (ledger row 960).
- A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, is a `ZZ64` (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
- `u =/= 0` is `true` for a zero `u` of `NN32`, `NN64` or `RR32`, and so is `q =/= 0.5` for `q: QQ = 1/2` (ledger row 966). Write `NOT (u = 0)`.
- A numeral that rounds to an infinity at `RR32` or `RR64` gives `Infinity`, with no error (ledger row 967).
- A negative constant, as `-3` or `5 - 8`, at a program's own number type reaches its `coerce(x: NaturalNumeral)` with its sign, as a natural numeral of value -3, not as `-` on the coercion of 3 (ledger row 968).
- A body with a declared return type is not converted by coercion, except a numeral: `r(): Wide = NarrowOf(3)` returns the `NarrowOf` (ledger row 387). Write the value at the declared type.

## Where a fix of walk belongs

Both paths run the same desugaring phases. Inside them, switches in `Shell.java` decide which desugarings run. Walk turns off these desugarings, which the compiled path runs:
----
65:- It runs a program's own `coerce` from a numeral once for each place where the numeral is written, in the component class's static initializer, except at a generic type (below). So a coercion that raises stops the program before `run()`. A test of it sets `run_exits_nonzero=true` (`tests-writing.md`).
108:  - At a program's own generic type, a numeral's coercion runs at each evaluation (ledger row 957). Bind the value once, at a top-level variable.
111:  - As a `typecase`'s selector, a numeral keeps the type `IntLiteral`, so `typecase 7 of ZZ32 => ...` is refused as unreachable (ledger row 963). Bind the selector to a variable first, as `x = 7`, then write `typecase x of ...`.
----

## Fortress as a language

Each point below corrects an assumption from a language that you know. `references/tests-writing.md` gives the form of a program.

- **Dispatch is on every argument, at run time.** A call chooses among overloads by the run-time types of all its arguments, as in Julia, not by static types as in Java. The checker accepts two overloads only if their parameter types exclude each other, one is strictly more specific, or a third covers their meet. The more specific one's return type must fit the other's. Walk checks part of this at load.
- **Functional methods.** A method with `self` among its parameters is called `f(x)`, not `x.f()`. It overloads with top-level functions. Most operators are declared so: `opr +(self, other: T): T`. A functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports it, so do not name a variable after it. One type must not have a dotted and a functional method of the same name.
- **Traits and objects, no classes.** A trait has methods and abstract fields, and extends several traits. An object is a leaf. `excludes {A, B}` says that no value has both types. `comprises {A, B}` says that every value has a listed type, near Scala's `sealed`. No type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. This exclusion rule is why the number types are flat (below).
- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (a `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`: `references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`, but an expression of numerals alone folds exactly (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"). The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.
- **Loops and reductions are library code.** `for`, comprehensions and `SUM` call the library's generators and reductions (`references/library.md`).
- **Juxtaposition is an operator, and whitespace counts.** `f x` applies a function. Otherwise juxtaposition is an operator that the library overloads: `2 x` multiplies, and `"a" "b"` concatenates. How three juxtaposed items group depends on their types, unlike in Haskell. An infix operator has whitespace on both sides or on neither: `a -b` is a static error. Precedence is partial: `a + b ∪ c` needs parentheses.
- **Specified, but not built:** dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions and complex numbers. Some constructs run only under walk (`references/compiler.md`).

## Case 16: a numeral at an `NN32` binding

- **Trap.** Since climb batch 29 the default from Java, that a numeral binds to any integer type as a literal to `int`, is right, and the trap is the old answer, that walk refuses the binding. It is this key's answer until climb batch 29; the orientation's old rule, under walk a numeral is a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` "until walk runs the checker"; `tests-writing.md:34`, "Write `a: NN32 = unsigned(5)`, not `a: NN32 = 5`"; and the audit's A5, a numeral binds to `NN32` on neither path (`explorations/reviews/skills-distillation-audit.md:62`) (climb batch 29's `orientation/admission.md`, P-173's and F-341's rows). A second trap, for a test that checks the value: the three-argument `assert` taken to convert the numeral as the binding does.
- **Expected.** The binding works on both paths: `n: NN32 = 3` binds the `NN32` 3. A typed binding is a place that fixes a type, and the numeral converts there exactly from its value into `NN32` (P-173; F-341 under walk, F-342 compiled). Write it as it is. `unsigned(3)` and `(3).asNN32` give 3 too, but are not needed.

component NumeralTypeNoValueWalk

three: NaturalNumeral[\1, 10, 3\] = 3

(* A program's own type receives a numeral through a coercion generic over the numeral's four numbers, one value per place. *)
component NumeralOwnTypeWalk
export Executable

oneRounding(v: ZZ, r: ZZ32, m: ZZ32): RR64 =
    builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleDoubleArith.numeralToDouble")

value object CC64(re: RR64, im: RR64)
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = CC64(oneRounding(v, r.asZZ32, 0), 0.0)
    coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) =
        CC64(oneRounding(v, r.asZZ32, m.asZZ32), 0.0)
    opr +(self, other: CC64): CC64 = CC64(re + other.re, im + other.im)
    opr juxtaposition(self, other: CC64): CC64 =
        CC64(re other.re - im other.im, re other.im + im other.re)
end

i: CC64 = CC64(0.0, 1.0)

exact(d: RR64): QQ = do
    bits: ZZ64 = d.rawBits
    e: ZZ64 = (bits RSHIFT 52) BITAND 2047
    f: ZZ64 = bits BITAND 4503599627370495
    mant: ZZ = big(f + 4503599627370496)
    k: ZZ32 = (e - 1075).asZZ32
    two: ZZ = big(2)
    if k >= 0 then (mant two^k) / big(1) else mant / two^(-k) end
  end

value object Iv(lo: RR64, hi: RR64)
    coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = do
        q: QQ = v / r^(m.asZZ32)
        d: RR64 = oneRounding(v, r.asZZ32, m.asZZ32)
        a: QQ = exact(d)
        if a = q then Iv(d, d) elif q < a then Iv(d.nextDown, d) else Iv(d, d.nextUp) end
      end
end

value object BF16(bits: ZZ32)
    coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = do
        q: QQ = v / r^(m.asZZ32)
        half: QQ = 1/2
        s: QQ = q (128/1)
        k0: ZZ = floor(s)
        rest: QQ = s - (k0/1)
        up: Boolean = if rest > half then true elif rest < half then false else odd(k0) end
        k: ZZ = if up then k0 + 1 else k0 end
        BF16((k - 128 + 16256).asZZ32)
      end
end

value object Dec(unscaled: ZZ, scale: ZZ32)
    coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = Dec(v, m.asZZ32)
end

    var k: ZZ := v
    var j: ZZ32 := 0
    while k > big(0) OR j < n do

content.content:
1:# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild
7:: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.
48:The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:
57:- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
62:## The caches
64:All the caches are gitignored. A caches folder also holds:
66:- `environment_cache/`: another cache of walk's.
67:- `nativewrapper_cache/`: the wrappers for the Java classes that an api imports with `import java`.
68:- `global.map`: the linker's saved state, an empty map in practice. If it is missing, the linker writes an empty one, also in a private caches folder.
69:- `implementation.stamp`: the stamp of the build that the caches belong to ("Building", below).
71:Only these runs read `default_repository/caches`: `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`), `ant testOnly`, and a direct walk run. These runs use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), and need neither the library order nor warm caches: `harness-one.sh`, the gate's ladder regression (`gate.md`) and both ant suites. `harness-one.sh` keeps its private cache beside its scratch folder between calls (`tests-running.md`).
77:Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:
79:- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
91:Before the first compiled run, check that `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` holds five jars: `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar` and `CompilerSystem.jar`, which has no prefix. Sometimes all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known.
95:- Keep the caches in this case too. Once, emptying them made the jars, but a deletion hides the cause.
103:- If paths behave wrongly, read `repository/ProjectProperties.java`. It resolves `FORTRESS_HOME`, `BASEDIR` and the cache paths.
111:- It decides by a stamp whether it deletes the caches. `ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp` is a hash of the built implementation, and each caches folder holds the stamp of the build that filled it. At its end, the build keeps `default_repository/caches` if its stamp equals the new one, and empties it if not. It does not touch a private caches folder. It prints `Caches <folder> kept` or `Caches <folder> started again, empty`. The comment "The caches and the implementation" in `build.xml` gives the rule.
112:- `ant cleanCache` deletes the caches, whatever their stamp.
114:- After a build that started the caches again, yours or a test target's, run the library order before the next compiled run. So each edit of Java or Scala costs about 2 to 3 minutes before a compiled run: the build, then the library order.
133:If you see either, do the step now: recompile the component, or run the library order. Do not delete the caches to fix it. A deletion works only because it repeats the library order and every analysis from cold. If something else looks like a stale cache, find its cause before you delete anything.

(* The static numerals: a negative constant through the type's own minus, a generic program type, a static expression through a coercion from QQ, the defaults, and no numeral value at run time. *)
component NumeralStaticDesignWalk
import Reflect.{ typeOf }
export Executable

oneRounding(v: ZZ, r: ZZ32, m: ZZ32): RR64 =
    builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleDoubleArith.numeralToDouble")

value object CC64(re: RR64, im: RR64)
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = CC64(oneRounding(v, r.asZZ32, 0), 0.0)
    coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) =
        CC64(oneRounding(v, r.asZZ32, m.asZZ32), 0.0)
    opr -(self): CC64 = CC64(-re, -im)
    opr +(self, other: CC64): CC64 = CC64(re + other.re, im + other.im)
    opr -(self, other: CC64): CC64 = CC64(re - other.re, im - other.im)
    opr juxtaposition(self, other: CC64): CC64 =
        CC64(re other.re - im other.im, re other.im + im other.re)
end

i: CC64 = CC64(0.0, 1.0)

value object Tally(k: ZZ32, seen: ZZ, negated: Boolean)
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = Tally(v.asZZ32, v, false)
    opr -(self): Tally = Tally(-k, seen, true)
end

object Gen[\T\](v: ZZ)
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = Gen[\T\](v)
end

site(): Gen[\RR64\] = 3

value object Half(lo: QQ)
    coerce(q: QQ) = Half(q)
end

object Cell[\T\](c: T) end

value object Byte(b: ZZ32)
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) where { v < 256 } = Byte(v.asZZ32)
end

isZZ32(a: Any): Boolean = typecase a of ZZ32 => true; else => false end
isCellZZ32(a: Any): Boolean = typecase a of Cell[\ZZ32\] => true; else => false end

run(): () = do
    t: Tally = -3
    assert(t.k, -3, "-3 at Tally is Tally's minus on the coercion of 3")
    assert(t.seen, big(3), "the coercion sees the written numeral 3, without its sign")
    assert(t.negated, "Tally's own minus ran on -3")
    c: CC64 = -3 - 4 i
    assert(c.re SEQV -3.0, "-3 - 4 i has the real part -3.0")
    assert(c.im SEQV -4.0, "-3 - 4 i has the imaginary part -4.0")
    c3: CC64 = -3.5
    assert((c3.re SEQV -3.5) AND (c3.im SEQV -0.0), "-3.5 at CC64 is CC64's minus on the coercion of 3.5")
    z: ZZ32 = -2147483648
    assert(z + 2147483647, -1, "-2147483648 at ZZ32 folds exactly, then converts")
    r: RR64 = -0.0
    assert(r.rawBits, -9223372036854775808, "-0.0 at RR64 is IEEE's negative zero")
    assert((1/r).isInfinite AND (1/r) < 0, "1/r is -Infinity for r: RR64 = -0.0")
    assert(site() SEQV site(), "a numeral at a program's generic type is one object per place")
    g1: Gen[\RR64\] = 3
    g2: Gen[\RR64\] = 3
    assert(NOT (g1 SEQV g2), "two places at a program's generic type give two objects")
    assert(g1.v, big(3), "g: Gen of RR64 = 3 sees the value 3")
    h: Half = 10/20
    assert(h.lo = 1/2, "10/20 at a type with a coercion from QQ reaches it as the QQ 1/2")
    assert(0.1_2 SEQV 0.5, "0.1_2 SEQV 0.5")
    assert(NOT (0.1 = 0.1_16), "0.1 = 0.1_16 is false")
    q: QQ = 0.1
    assert(numerator(q), big(1), "q: QQ = 0.1 is exactly 1/10")
    assert(denominator(q), big(10), "q: QQ = 0.1 is exactly 1/10")
    f: RR64 = 0.1
    assert(f.rawBits, 4591870180066957722, "f: RR64 = 0.1 rounds once")
    y: Byte = 255
    assert(y.b, 255, "255 at a byte type whose coercion holds v < 256")
    x = 3
    assert(isZZ32(x), "x = 3 is a ZZ32")
    assert(isCellZZ32(Cell(3)), "Cell(3) is a Cell of ZZ32")
    assert(typeOf(3).asString, "ZZ32", "typeOf(3) shows no numeral type")

trait Number excludes { String }
value object Infinity extends Number end
value object NegativeInfinity extends Number end
value object IndefiniteNumber extends Number end
trait ZZ extends { Number, Equality[\ZZ\] } excludes { RR64, ZZ64, ZZ32, NN32, NN64 } 
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\])
    coerce(x: ZZ32)
    coerce(x: ZZ64)
    coerce(x: NN32)
    coerce(x: NN64)
trait ZZ64 extends { Number, Equality[\ZZ64\] } excludes { RR64 , ZZ }
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\])
    coerce(x: ZZ32) 
trait ZZ32 extends { Number, Equality[\ZZ32\], StandardTotalOrder[\ZZ32\] } excludes { ZZ64, RR32, RR64 }
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\])
trait NN32 extends { Number, Equality[\NN32\] } excludes { ZZ32, ZZ64, RR32, RR64 }
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\])
trait NN64 extends { Number, Equality[\NN64\] } excludes { ZZ32, ZZ64, RR32, RR64, NN32, ZZ }
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\])
    coerce(x: NN32)
trait Numeral extends Number excludes { ZZ, ZZ32, ZZ64, NN32, NN64, RR32, RR64 } end
trait AnyNaturalNumeral extends Numeral excludes { AnyRadixPointNumeral } end
trait AnyRadixPointNumeral extends Numeral end
trait NaturalNumeral[\nat n, nat r, nat v\] extends AnyNaturalNumeral end
trait RadixPointNumeral[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\] extends AnyRadixPointNumeral end
trait RR64 extends { Number, Equality[\RR64\] } excludes ZZ64
    coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\])
    coerce(x: RR32)
trait RR32 extends { Number, Equality[\RR32\] } excludes { ZZ64, ZZ32, RR64 }
    coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\])
trait Boolean   extends { Equality[\Boolean\], Condition[\()\] }

**Edit 1.** Head it with P-173's rule: **A numeral converts where it stands (P-173).** Cite P-174, P-76, P-172 and P-40 where each applies. State these points:

- Its own type, in the interpreter's library, is `NaturalNumeral`, or with a radix point `RadixPointNumeral`. Both are below `Numeral`, a sibling of the number types under `Number`, and the value holds the numeral's exact value. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude names them `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral`.
- Where its place fixes a type, the numeral converts into that type from its exact value. The places are a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter and a declared return type. A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as each of the eight number types has. The conversion is exact into the five integer types and `QQ`, and rounds once into `RR64` and `RR32`. So `u: NN32 = 5` binds, `q: QQ = 0.1` is `1/10`, and `h = 0.5` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`.
- Elsewhere the numeral takes its default: `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where its value does not fit, and `RR64` with a radix point. Elsewhere means an untyped binding, `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, `Index`, an unbounded type parameter. So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, `n = 3000000000` a `ZZ64`, and `Cell(0.5)` a `Cell[\RR64\]`. The default is the value's type from then on: for `x = 0.1`, `q: QQ = x` is refused. A type parameter that numerals alone fix takes the narrowest default that holds them all. Optional: a bare float numeral prints as its double, so `"" 2.50` is `"2.5"`.
- Out of range at a typed place, the numeral is refused: by the checker statically, and by walk when it runs.
- A `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`, so `u: NN32 = n` is refused (P-173, P-40).
- Write a numeral type only as the parameter type of a coercion or an operator (P-174). The checker refuses it as a variable's, field's or return type. A program's own number type receives a numeral through its own `coerce(x: NaturalNumeral)` or `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`, with one result per site. Without such a coercion, the type refuses a numeral. Do not state how a negative numeral reaches that coercion: item 448 is open.

# Climb batch 29b: orientation admission Nine entries are admitted. They make three edits, all in "Numbers": 1. **A program's own number type takes a numeral through a coercion generic over the numeral's numbers, and no numeral value exists when a program runs (P-174, F-79, F-342, P-173, P-40, P-37, F-341).** This rewrites the rule "A numeral converts where it stands (P-173)" (`:89`) and its second paragraph (`:91`). 2. **No `=` ties a numeral type to a number type, and the numeral types declare no `asFloat` (P-165, F-346, F-341).** This corrects "`Number` declares nothing (P-165)" (`:99`) and deletes the example `(h = 0.5)` at `:89`. 3. **A folded expression reaches a program's own type only through its coercion from the folded value's type (P-174).** This qualifies "An expression of numerals alone folds exactly" (`:93`). The landing is climb batch 29b, the static numerals. It replaces the field numerals that climb batch 29 built and that the orientation now describes. The orientation was last changed at climb batch 29's landing, before the curator rewrote P-174, split out P-176 and added P-37's exception (`cac54a1bf1`), and before he scoped P-40's bound to sizes (`51b048ea1c`). So most sentences of `:89`, `:91` and `:99` that speak of the numeral's type are now false. RECORD.md, "Left for the coordinator and the skill writer", names `:89` with its `(h = 0.5)`. Rung A's REPORT.md, section 6, names `:91` and `:99`. The post-batch review, Part 3, items 2 to 4, names all three. Each was checked here against the tree, by reading and by four walk probes at `5f35b1d058`, run from a scratch folder with private caches and not kept. Their outputs are quoted in the rows. The defaults that these edits correct come from three sources: - **The orientation's own text.** It says that a numeral holds its exact value, that a program's coercion reads the getters `digits`, `fractionDigits`, `radix` and `digitValue`, that a compiled program writes `coerce(x: IntLiteral)`, that the numeral types declare `asFloat`, and that `(h = 0.5)` is `true`. - **The pretraining quiz.** It says that "`IntLiteral` is the type of integer literals", and that a literal type "coerces to the context's type. This allows `x: RR64 = 3`" (`reviews/fortress-pretraining-quiz.md:156`, `:162`). - **The core.** "A `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`" (`SKILL.md:133`). The mistakes are on record. The batch rewrote eight of its own tests that were written to the old forms. Every one of the orientation's old coercion forms now stops under walk. Regression cases 16 and 26 now have wrong keys, and `interpreter.md:23` gives a workaround that answers wrongly. Every other entry falls in one of these groups: - It changed only its line citations: 30 FACTS entries and six POSITIONS entries. - It is a measure. - It is compiled-path or walk detail that an area part owns. Per the curator's comment of 2026-11-08 (`6ec749a8eb`), path behaviours go to `interpreter.md` and `compiler.md` as defects with their rows. - The orientation already states it. Several area parts and the core now hold false sentences. They are listed under "Elsewhere". **Inputs.** - The landing: base `b5b0f82c13`; rung A `a26e74f5c8` and rung T `fcfd0aeb31`; `c6ef2f0b80` (rows closed), `17e93a7da8` (the gather record), `eb8a592455` (the review's corrections), `a2be3e9e1d` (the gate's tables); the record landing, `36e60805e6` and `5f35b1d058`. Also read: - `compile-ladder/climb-batch-29b/RECORD.md`, all of it from "Rows opened"; - `record-landing/diff.md` and `owed.md`, "For the coordinator"; - `reviews/batch-29b-review.md`, Part 3; - `compile-ladder/rung-static-numerals/REPORT.md`, sections 1, 5, 6 and 11; - ledger rows 442, 957, 966, 971, 973 and 974; - review-queue items 487 to 489. - The orientation, 28,031 bytes (`wc -c`), read whole. Also read: `SKILL.md`, the prior orientation admission (`climb-batch-29/orientation/admission.md`), `interpreter.md:15-26` and `compiler.md:34`, `:65`, `:103-111`. - The evidence searched: - `tools/orientation/regression/key.md`, cases 5, 16, 26 and 31; - `reviews/fortress-pretraining-quiz.md:156`, `:162`, `:253`; - `git diff b5b0f82c13 HEAD` over `ProjectFortress/tests`, `compiler_tests` and `library_tests`, for test lines in the old numeral forms; - the prelude, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:90-450`, and the library's numeral types, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:455-470`. - The probes, under walk at `5f35b1d058`: - `n: NN32 = 3`, `u: NN32 = 0`, `q: QQ = 1/2` and `r: RR64 = 3` compared with numerals: `n = 3 ... false`, `u = 0 ... false`, `NOT (u = 0): true`, `u = z, z: NN32 = 0: true`, `q = 0.5 ... false`, `r = 3 ... true`; - a coercion `coerce(x: NaturalNumeral) = D(x.digitValue)`: 'Type requires static arguments: FortressLibrary.NaturalNumeral'; - the generic form, `= D(x.digitValue)`: 'Non-object receiver (): () trying to invoke method digitValue'; - the generic form, `= E(v)` for `value object E(k: ZZ32)`: 'Unification error: Closure/Constructor for E param 1 ($k:ZZ32) got arg 7:ZZ of type ZZ'; - `t: Tally = 2 + 3`, for a `Tally` that has only its numeral coercion: 'RHS expression type ZZ32 is not assignable to LHS type Tally', where `a: Tally = 5` gave 5. **The test.** An entry is admitted only if a worker would act differently without it, and the mistake that it prevents has evidence: a failure on record, the regression quiz, or the pretraining quiz. Its `:91`: "A program's own number type receives a numeral through its own `coerce(x: NaturalNumeral)` or `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`. Its static arguments are the numeral's numbers: the digit count, the digits after the point, the radix, and the digits read as one integer in that radix.
